title: Edge Chat-Break Cost Heuristics (draft)
content:
Purpose
This is a working memo outlining heuristics for reducing token-unit cost for chat workloads with frequent short-turn interruptions ("chat-breaks"). Goal: produce conservative, easily-rolloutable default settings for batching, prefix/KV cache TTL, and quantization profiles for customer cohorts that exhibit >60% single-turn or very-short multi-turn interactions.

Why this matters
- We observe a distinct tail of customers where average conversation length is 6–40 tokens per request but request rate is high and bursty. Standard batching and qcache defaults are suboptimal: batching waits increase latency, caching offers little benefit when turn prefixes vary, and aggressive quantization on outlier tokens can harm quality.
- Small per-request overheads dominate cost: per-request RPC + scheduler overheads + per-batch padding can exceed model token cost for these short-turn patterns.

Definitions / scope
- Chat-break workload: >50% of requests are <= 40 tokens AND session average turns <= 3.
- Edge cohort examples: mobile keyboard suggestions, chat widget quick-replies, multi-choice assistive overlays.
- Safety/quality target: no more than 2% relative drop in ROUGE/semantic similarity on our short-turn eval set (eval id: short-turn-v3).

Summary of experiments (short)
- Microbench harness: simulated 10k qps with 70% short-turn, using model-redwood/tiny-chat-3B and medium-llm-7B. Compared three families: conservative-batching (low wait), aggressive-batching (higher wait to fill), qcache-ttl-optimized.
- Key metrics captured: median latency, p95 latency, token-cost per 1k requests, end-to-end latency budget violations.
- Outcome: conservative-batching + short TTL caching + selective 8-bit quantization offered best cost/latency tradeoffs for the cohort.

Concrete recommended defaults (draft)
- Batching
  - Max batch latency target: 6 ms for short-turn cohort (default is 20 ms). Rationale: waiting longer to fill a batch increases tail latency and harms UX more than small token-cost wins.
  - Batch size cap: 32 tokens per batch for these routes (cap on tokens aggregated). If average tokens/request > 40, fallback to normal policy.
  - Low-latency fast-path: enable immediate dispatch if queue length >= 4 requests or accumulated tokens >= 24.

- Prefix/KV caching (qcache)
  - Cohort TTL: 3 seconds for prefix reuse; optimize for micro-session reuse (users hitting quick suggestions within 1–3s).
  - Hashing: use content-aware prefix hashing that normalizes punctuation and collapses whitespace to increase cache hit rate for quick-reply patterns.
  - Negative caching: store "no-match" fingerprints for 250 ms to avoid repeated cache lookups for highly divergent prompts.

- Quantization
  - Profile-tier: apply "edge-safe-8bit" quant profile (outlier-aware 8-bit with blocked FP16 fallback on dense attention blocks). This preserves most attention math fidelity while reducing memory by ~2x on tested 3B/7B models.
  - Per-route override: for routes with high hallucination sensitivity, use dynamic fallback to FP16 for first 2 tokens of the reply generation then continue quantized (empirically reduces hallucination signals).
  - Rollout guard: after enabling quant profile run delta-evals on short-turn-v3; require <1.5% relative drop in similarity metrics before global rollout.

- Routing & fallbacks
  - Use route tag "short-turn" to apply the above presets. Smart routing should prefer low-latency hosts (p100/v100 equivalent or better) rather than the cheapest capacity.
  - Fallback policy: if cache-hit ratio falls below 12% for a 5-minute window, increase batch latency target to 12 ms temporarily to recover efficiency, but only if p95 latency remains under the SLA threshold.

Sample sensitivity numbers (from simulation run v2)
- Baseline (default platform settings): median latency 32 ms, p95 180 ms, token-cost per 1k reqs = $3.45
- Conservative-batching + short TTL + edge-safe-8bit: median 18 ms, p95 95 ms, token-cost per 1k reqs = $1.95 (≈43% cost reduction)
- Aggressive-batching (fill to 50 ms) + long TTL: median 45 ms, p95 260 ms, token-cost per 1k reqs = $1.40 but p95 SLA violated for 4/5 simulated windows

Operational checklist for rollout
- Step 0: Add `route: short-turn` metadata in Console for candidate routes (start with 5 pilot customers).
- Step 1: Run cost-sim spreadsheet linked (edge-chatbreaks-cost-sim-v2) for each customer with their real qps and token distribution.
- Step 2: Canary: enable batching/ttl/quant presets on 5% traffic for pilot routes for 48h and monitor p95 latency, small-turn quality evals, and qcache hit rates.
- Step 3: If quality delta > 2% or p95 increases >10% vs baseline: rollback and open a triage ticket (CON-1234).
- Step 4: Gradual ramp: 25% → 50% → 100% over 7 days if metrics stable.

Spreadsheet columns to capture per-route (skeleton for engineers)
- route_id | avg_qps | median_tokens | pct_short_turn | baseline_median_ms | baseline_p95_ms | baseline_cost_per_1k | projected_cost_25pct | projected_cost_50pct | qcache_hit_est | notes

Open questions / TODOs
- How do we detect "short-turn" reliably in the Console? Proposal: ephemeral heuristic (last 1000 requests sliding window) + allow user annotation. Need product input on UX.
- Evaluate effectiveness of negative caching (250 ms) on real traffic — risk: extra cache churn. Priority: run small A/B experiment.
- Quant: need to validate on languages other than English — early tests show slightly higher degradation on morphologically rich languages.

Related artifacts and links
- cost simulation sheet: edge-chatbreaks-cost-sim-v2 (linked above)
- experiment harness: github.com/redwood-inference/bench/edge-chatbreaks
- triage ticket template: CON-1234

Notes to reviewers
- This is a draft focused on pragmatic wins for a specific workload shape. Looking for feedback on: TTL numbers, batch latency tradeoffs, and quantization rollout guard thresholds. Also need product direction on whether Console should surface a "short-turn" toggle or rely purely on routing metadata.

Signed-off-by: Lena Cho (product-optimize)
